column5: 14z-167: file a ticket - tenant attack records with facing rule +0xE = 5 are XORed into the victim's facing by vsavj's hit code (Killshread Summon (ES) moves Demitri on native only)
column10: Q3: resolved by WORK, and the finding was true: the p2step field was sampled as a BYTE (ff8964:b) while the counter +0x164 is a WORD (move.w $164(a6) at vs2 0x27050), so the instrument read the high byte and never registered the slide - the exclusion of the step table is WITHDRAWN. Re-traced as ff8964:w on both legs (build/x_family_14z167/step_routine_and_trace.txt, run7.log): the counter runs 0 -> 20 over 3928-3944 on BOTH legs with index +0x59 = 2 (the 80 px / 20 f list), and the step routine (vs2 0x27038, disassembled in the same file) picks the sign from +0x5D: tst.b $5d(a6); bne -> add, else neg.w. Native's rule-5 resolution writes 0 on the second wave, so the 20 steps are negated and Demitri slides 835 -> 755 toward Donovan; ours' XOR writes 4, nonzero, so the same steps are ADDED, away from Donovan, and his x holds at 835 (what holds it there - the stage edge - is not measured). The mover is therefore identified: the pushback step table, run identically on both legs, signed by the facing byte the two resolvers wrote differently. The ticket's text carries this corrected mechanism.

(a) NO GATE EVER OPENED THE SHIPPED FILE: the browser gate regenerated the page into its own workdir and drove that, and the sibling gate compared two fresh generations to each other, so "the shipped page is that generation" was assumed by everything. A hand-edited page, or a generator change landed without re-packaging, would have passed every check. FIXED TWO WAYS: test_applier_page.sh now regenerates EVERY platform dir's page and requires release/

/apply_release.html to be byte-identical to it (3/3 dirs), and test_applier_page_browser.sh now loads the SHIPPED file itself rather than a fresh one. (b) The fidelity leg runs through apply_node.mjs, which the page does not contain, so the page's own WIRING (page_shell.html's calls into the modules) was never compared with the tool of record. That gap is now NAMED in the gate's header and is covered from the other side: the browser gate drives the shipped page's real wiring — drop zone, radio, button — and checks the set key it prints, which is a SHA-1 over every member name and every member byte. Stated rather than overclaimed: the browser leg checks the set key, not member-for-member. Q4: TRUE, and the sharpest of the three: the "no network primitive" guarantee rested on a denylist of seven names with ONE control, and the page itself proved the blind spot by carrying `link.href = URL.createObjectURL(...)`, which the scan cannot see. A denylist cannot prove absence. RESOLVED BY CHANGING THE MECHANISM, not by lengthening the list: the page now carries a Content-Security-Policy of `default-src 'none'; connect-src 'none'; form-action 'none'; base-uri 'none'` (plus frame/object/worker), so the BROWSER refuses every network primitive including the ones nobody enumerated, and the generator REFUSES to emit a page whose CSP is missing or weakened. The CSP is not decorative and was proven enforced the hard way: the browser gate's own driver, which lived inside the document, stopped working with "Failed to fetch" the moment the CSP landed — so the driver was rewritten as a SEPARATE page that iframes the shipped file, which keeps the page's real policy intact during the test instead of diluting it to be testable. The denylist is kept as an independent authoring-time check and was widened to the five primitives the checker named (RTCPeerConnection, WebTransport, Worker/SharedWorker, serviceWorker, setAttribute of a URL attribute, plus fetchLater, RTCDataChannel, new Image, geolocation), and a SECOND control `page-without-csp` now fires on a different mechanism from `page-with-fetch`. Q4's second limb — a refusal string present but unreachable — is also true: that leg IS a presence test, it now says so in the gate's own output and header, and the exercised cases went from four to SIX (a modified dump, a truncated dump, a missing dump, a dump with an extra member, a corrupted patch, a tampered manifest), each requiring both tools to refuse, both to name the same thing, and neither to write. ALSO MEASURED AND REJECTED while resolving Q4: Chrome's `--log-net-log` was tried as a direct "the page made zero network requests" measurement. It is NOT usable — the netlog records the BROWSER's own traffic (variations seed, component update, account listing, the default new-tab page), 15 non-file:// URLs on a default profile and still 9 with every background-networking flag disabled, none of them the page's. An assertion built on filtering Chrome's own requests would be an instrument that lies, so it was dropped rather than tuned. Q5: TRUE, and it is a PACKET-CONSTRUCTION error rather than a false claim. The claim attributes two closures to the maintainer and the artifact list contained no document carrying their words; the checker was right to refuse the attribution from what it was given. The words exist and are recorded verbatim, quoted, and dated in DECISIONS_HISTORY.md ("Ruled 2026-09-21 (14z-174) — #146 CLOSED", *"README is good enough for now. It may be improved, but it will be on the basis of more user feedback"*; and "Ruled 2026-09-21 (14z-174) — #144 CLOSED as MITIGATED, NOT ELIMINATED", *"Indeed, closeable with an explicit comment as mitigated not solved."*), and in each issue's closing comment. The lesson is the packet's: WHEN A PACKET ATTRIBUTES A DECISION, THE DECISION RECORD IS AN ARTIFACT. Recorded as a gotcha rather than left in this ledger row. The second limb — "the remaining M19 blocker list is empty but for #145" — is withdrawn as a claim of this packet: it is a consequence of the two closures plus the maintainer's own words about environments, and it belongs in the close's recommendation with those words quoted, not in a fidelity packet whose artifacts are code.
